amendments.rule: **An age written with `בֶּן` gives the English *old* to that noun.** Hebrew states an age as `בֶּן` with a numeral, usually with `שָׁנָה` standing after it, and the ASV writes *X years old*: the `בֵּן` takes the *old*, the numeral takes its own word, and `שָׁנָה` takes the *years* as the counted noun, which rule 22 places where a compound numeral distributes it. Do not mark the `בֵּן` `unrepresented` on the ground that no English word writes *son*, and do not fuse the phrase under rule 30: each morpheme has an English word of its own, so rule 2 splits them, and the subtraction test rules 16, 31 and 43 use finds the statement of age gone with the *old* while the numeral and the counted noun are left saying only how many years. The unit is discontinuous under rule 25 wherever the counted noun stands between, which in English is always, since Hebrew writes the `בֵּן` before its numeral and the ASV writes the *old* after the years. The corpus aligns `בֵּן` to *old* in a hundred and four units, to *was old* in twenty-eight, to *a old* in ten and to *being old* in five, and heads every one of them on the word carrying the age, so this is settled rather than a tie to hedge. Three riders. Where the clause is verbless and the ASV writes a copula, that word is the predicate's and joins the `בֵּן` unit under rule 20, which is what those *was old* units are. Where a preposition stands before the `בֵּן` it takes whatever the ASV writes for it under rule 11, as `מִבֶּן עֶשְׂרִים שָׁנָה` → ***from*** *twenty years old* does, and where the ASV leaves that relation unstated the preposition is `unrepresented` under rule 40 as usual. And this governs the age construction only: a `בֵּן` naming a son, and the `בָּנִים` of a bird's young that the ASV writes *young*, are read by the ordinary rules. **And where the Hebrew writes no counted noun at all, the *years* the ASV supplies completes the numeral and is never `added`.** Hebrew states the same age without `שָׁנָה` as readily as with it — `בֶּן־שְׁלֹשִׁים וּשְׁתַּיִם הָיָה בְמָלְכוֹ` → *Thirty and two* ***years*** *old was he when he began to reign* — and there the numeral stands for what it counts, so the supplied noun joins that numeral's unit under rule 31's substantival numeral and the head stays on the numeral, which carries the lexeme. Read which numeral it joins as rule 22 reads a counted noun distributed across a compound figure: English writes the noun once after the whole figure, so the supplied *years* joins the last numeral of the Hebrew one, standing exactly where a written `שָׁנָה` would have stood. Do not mark it `added` under rule 20's supplied-lexical-verb clause or rule 33's supplied-phrase sentence, and do not fold it into the `בֵּן` beside it: what those clauses govern is English answering to no morpheme at all, and here the numeral the word completes is written. And read the Hebrew before reaching for this sentence, since a written `שָׁנָה` takes the *years* itself under this rule's first sentence, and one chapter may write both shapes, as 2CH.21.5 and 2CH.21.20 do.
amendments.why: Rule 58 presupposes `שָׁנָה` standing after the numeral ("usually with `שָׁנָה` standing after it") and then says only that `שָׁנָה` takes the *years*, which leaves the commonest variant of the regnal age formula undecided. 2CH.21.20 writes the age with no counted noun at all, so the ASV's *years* answers to no noun morpheme, and a pass reading rule 58 alone would either mark it `added` under rule 20 or fold it into `בֵּן`. Rule 31's substantival numeral already settles it in general terms — a generic noun supplied to complete a numeral standing for what it counts joins that numeral's unit and never moves the head — and rule 22's tail-to-tail reading settles which numeral takes it, so the rider records the crossing rather than inventing a treatment. No corpus row contradicts it: rule 31's own precedent is `אֶחָד` → *one portion* and `אֶחָד` → *the first day*, and the `בֵּן` corpus quoted in this rule bears only on the *old*, which is unchanged. Written as an amendment rather than a new rule so that the sentence saying `שָׁנָה` takes the *years* is qualified where it stands.

conventions: Phrasal verbs in this chapter are classified as rule 44's verb-plus-particle, not as light verb plus complement, and every one of them heads on the English verb: passed over, was risen up, rose up, compassed about, carried away, brake into, came up, stirred up, fall out, fell out, led astray. What puts a rendering in the other class is a lexical complement that carries the source verb's lexeme, as in zanah hiphil rendered made ... to play the harlot (21.11, 21.13), headed on play. A directional or resultative adverb standing beside the verb is not such a complement, however imperfectly the bare English verb writes the lexeme: shavah rendered carried away and nadach rendered led astray both head on the verb. 21.11 was corrected from astray to led in the chapter reconciliation pass.

The regnal accession formula be-malkho is rendered when he began to reign at 21.5 and 21.20 and is divided identically in both: the beth takes when under rule 52, the suffix on the infinitive construct takes the subject pronoun he under rule 18, and began is read as part of the infinitive's own rendering rather than as a supplied lexical verb, so the infinitive holds began to reign, headed on reign. The inchoative is what the ASV writes for this Hebrew formula everywhere in Kings and Chronicles; no corpus query was run for it in this pass, so a later chapter finding contrary precedent should record it rather than assume this.

report: One real cross-verse split, in the phrasal verbs. The chapter heads a Hebrew verb rendered by an English verb plus a directional adverb on the verb in ten places (21.4 was risen up, 21.9 passed over / rose up / compassed about, 21.15 fall out, 21.16 stirred up, 21.17 came up / brake into / carried away, 21.19 fell out) and on the particle once, at 21.11, nadach rendered led ASTRAY. Rule 44 keeps the head on the verb for exactly this shape, since forth and away name nothing on their own, and 21.17 carried away for shavah is the same construction decided the other way in this same chapter. 21.11 is patched to head on t022 (led), with astray named in the unit note as the competing head.

Everything else in the candidate table is context rather than a split. The possessive have goes to whatever makes the clause possessive in all three shapes: lamed at 21.2, the written hayah at 21.6 with its preposition unrepresented, and the predicate beth at 21.15 (rules 43, 49). ben takes old at 21.5 and 21.20, the copula joining ben in the verbless 21.5 while the written hayah takes was he at 21.20. The two determiner phrases at 21.10 differ only in how many determiners the ASV wrote, and both run the rule 41/47 count. derekh is a plain construct noun throughout and never rule 19's toward case. The regnal be-malkho is identical at 21.5 and 21.20.

Fusions checked and left standing: kaasher to as (21.6, 21.7), tachat asher to Because (21.12), ki im to save (21.17), al yad to beside (21.16), be-lo to without (21.20), le-ein marpe to incurable (21.18), and kol ha-yamim to alway with the article unrepresented (21.7), which is rule 30's own chronicles treatment. The single noncompositional unit, 21.19 le-yamim mi-yyamim to in process of time, stands: no allocation of in, process, of and time across the four morphemes is independently defensible, and the note says so. 21.3 first born is a genuine tie, left as the verse pass took it with the competing head named.

No unit in the chapter is marked added, so I read every supplied English word for a wrongly folded one. Each is licensed: Now when (rule 55) and so that (rule 55), the presentative frames at 21.12, 21.17 and 21.19 (rules 17, 21, 45), by night and with a great plague and the of before thy father's house (rule 33), high places and precious things (rule 31), the supplied the on construct nouns (rule 29), and the years supplied at 21.20 where the Hebrew writes no shanah (rule 31, now written into rule 58 by the amendment below).

BSB disagreements: none is a genuine error. The ten R rows are the documented convention difference, being prepositions the ASV's recasting leaves nothing to say (the four beth phrases of 21.14 promoted to direct objects of smite, the dative lamed of 21.3 and 21.17, the lamed of lemor at 21.12); the two et rows are rule 16; the 21.4 and 21.19 waws are correctly unrendered under rules 14 and 45; the three 21.10 articles are the determiner count; and the 21.19 et and tset are a real ASV compression of ke-eth tseth ha-qets rather than a misplaced edge. I reviewed that compression against rule 30's fusion and left it split, since qets plainly owns end while the periphrasis is simply dropped.
